name: Hyaluronic acid

lead: Hyaluronic acid is a sugar-based molecule found in skin and joints that binds large amounts of water. In serums it gives temporary surface hydration and a plumper look; in cross-linked injectable gels it is used as a dermal filler to add volume to lips, cheeks, under-eyes and folds.

Topical products hydrate the outer skin layer, which smooths the look of fine lines for a time. Fillers physically add volume, with an effect that Wikipedia says lasts around 6 to 12 months, and they have US FDA regulatory approval. A 2022 review examined topical HA for skin quality and aging, and small trials have tested oral HA supplements.

paras: Serums are applied to damp skin once or twice daily and layered under moisturizer, often alongside other actives. Fillers are administered in a clinic by trained injectors, with results visible right away and refreshed periodically as they gradually dissolve.

Topical forms are very well tolerated. Fillers commonly cause short-lived bruising, swelling and lumps at the injection site. Rare severe complications include vascular occlusion leading to tissue damage or vision loss, and outcomes are associated with injector skill.

chain: Smoother-looking skin and fewer fine lines
angle.text: Hyaluronic acid serums give temporary hydration and plumping, while injectable fillers reshape lips, cheeks and the under-eye area. It binds water, so skin looks fuller and fine lines look softer. Topical use gives short-lived hydration in studies, and fillers have extensive clinical use for volume.

lead: Hyaluronic acid (HA, hyaluronan) is a long-chain sugar polymer, an anionic, non-sulfated glycosaminoglycan, found throughout connective, epithelial and neural tissue. An average 70 kg person holds roughly 15 grams, about a third of which turns over each day, and it is a major component of the extracellular matrix, synovial fluid and cartilage [1]. Its carboxylate groups carry a negative charge that lets it bind water, which is why it features in so many cosmetic products [1].

HA is used to improve appearance in three main ways. Cross-linked HA gels are injected as dermal fillers to add volume or smooth lines in the lips, cheeks, chin, nasolabial folds, under-eye hollows and the backs of the hands; the effect is visible straight away and typically lasts around 6 to 12 months before the body breaks the gel down [1][2][3]. Topical serums and creams use HA as a humectant to hydrate the skin surface, giving a smoother, plumper-looking skin quality [4]. Oral supplements, often combined with collagen and vitamin C, are sold for skin hydration and density [5][6].

Research covers all three. Systematic reviews of filler trials report that most adverse events are short-lived injection-site reactions, while rare severe complications such as vascular occlusion can occur [7][8][3]. Topical HA has been studied in short randomised trials of hydration and wrinkles [4], and oral HA in small randomised trials [6][5]. Appearance communities discuss HA mainly as a filler and as a joint supplement [9][10][11][12].

paras: Dermal fillers. Most HA fillers are cross-linked, usually with the cross-linker BDDE, so that the gel resists the enzymes that would otherwise clear natural HA within about half a day [2][13]. They are injected with a fine needle or a blunt cannula, and the water-binding gel adds volume [1]. Uses include lip enhancement, nasolabial folds, perioral lines, cheek and chin contouring and under-eye hollows, plus the back of the hand [14][15][3]. Juvederm and Restylane are the two best-known product families [13][15][7].

Skin boosters and micro-fillers. Trials have studied HA-based micro-fillers placed in the skin for superficial wrinkles and skin quality, including a randomised prospective multicentre study, and a split-face comparison of polynucleotide and HA fillers around the eyes [16][17].

Topical products. HA appears in serums, moisturisers and masks. The EU cosmetic ingredient database lists it with skin-conditioning and humectant functions [1]. A 2022 review in Dermatologic Therapy, co-authored by L'Oreal-affiliated researchers, discusses how molecular weight shapes behaviour: higher-molecular-weight HA mostly forms a hydrating film on the surface, while lower-molecular-weight forms are described as reaching deeper layers [4].
Oral supplements. HA is sold alone or with collagen and vitamin C for skin condition [5][6][18].

HA injections are used for knee osteoarthritis (viscosupplementation). Network meta-analyses and trials have compared HA with corticosteroids and platelet-rich plasma in knee and hip osteoarthritis, and a systematic review addressed temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis [19][20][21][22]. HA viscoelastic products are used in eye surgery, beginning with Healon in the 1970s and 1980s, and registered trials cover products such as Healon5, DisCoVisc and Monovisc [1][23][24][25][26]. Wikipedia states that reviews as of 2023 found limited evidence for HA in chronic wound healing [1]. A trial tested HA gel with photobiomodulation after gingivectomy [27].

Karl Meyer and John Palmer isolated HA from the vitreous humor of a cow's eye in 1934, and named it from the Greek hyalos, glass-like, plus uronic acid [1][13]. For decades it was regarded as an inert, gluey substance, until work showed specific roles in tissues [1]. Pharmacia developed Healon, the first hyaluronan biomedical product, approved for eye surgery in the 1970s and 1980s [1]. Animal sources such as rooster combs were the main supply, with microbial fermentation developed later because of low yield, cost and ethical concerns [1].

Fillers before HA included paraffin around 1900, liquid silicone from the early 1960s and bovine collagen from around 1980, which became the benchmark for later products but needed an allergy test [14]. HA was approved for facial tissue augmentation in Europe in 1996 according to Wikipedia, and Restylane is described as the first HA filler approved by the FDA for cosmetic injection [13][15]. Juvederm gained FDA approval in June 2006, supported by trials including a 146-subject, 24-week comparison with a collagen filler [13]. The American Society of Plastic Surgeons reported 778,000 Restylane injections in 2006 [14]. Since then HA has become the dominant filler material, with fillers regulated as medical devices [2][7].

HA fillers are gels in which HA chains are chemically linked, so the material holds shape and resists breakdown. Their properties, such as firmness and spread, depend on cross-linking and rheology [28]. A 2024 clinical review examined the injectability of cross-linked HA fillers, including the force needed to inject and differences between products [29].

The result is temporary because the body gradually metabolises the gel, and physical activity may shorten it [2]. HA fillers can be dissolved with the enzyme hyaluronidase, which Wikipedia describes as the recommended way to remove HA filler for complications, and which is used in other fields to help drugs disperse in tissue [30]. Wikipedia lists HA among the most common filler materials, partly because it occurs naturally in vertebrates and is biodegradable [2].

Filler. Randomised trials generally compare products with each other or with controls and form the basis for regulatory approval [7][8][16]. The 2022 Dermatologic Therapy review notes that exogenous HA is cleared and degraded quickly in skin [4].

Topical. The Dermatologic Therapy review summarises randomised trials: a 30-day trial in 40 women reported improvement versus placebo across six HA types; a 60-day trial in 65 women with wrinkles around the eyes found that the two lowest-molecular-weight formulations significantly reduced wrinkle depth and improved elasticity; and a 24-week single-blind trial in 63 women compared a 1.5 percent HA serum plus botulinum toxin with the toxin alone, reporting differences of roughly 14 to 24 percent in fine lines, crow's feet, tone, texture, radiance and elasticity. The authors note that many studies are short or lack controls and call for longer controlled trials [4].

Oral. A 2023 trial randomised 129 healthy women in Shanghai to placebo or oral HA for up to 12 weeks, and reported higher skin hydration at weeks 2 to 8, improved skin tone, and, at one dose, greater epidermal thickness; dermal density fell in the placebo group but not the treated groups. Three authors were affiliated with the HA supplier [6]. A 2024 trial of 87 women over 16 weeks found that collagen plus vitamin C, with or without 30 mg HA, improved dermal density, texture and wrinkle severity, with no significant change in elasticity or hydration and no added effect from HA over collagen alone [5][5]. A 2025 meta-analysis addressed collagen supplements and skin hydration and elasticity [18].

Common reactions after filler are bruising, redness, swelling, pain, tenderness and itching; less common are nodules, granulomas, infection and allergic reactions [2][3]. A 2023 Cureus meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials found swelling, lumps and firmness more common at the nasolabial fold than at the midface, perioral or lip regions, while pain, redness, bruising and itching did not differ by site [7]. A 2024 systematic review of 48 randomised trials grouped events into expected reactions, product- or technique-related events and severe events, found most short-lived and self-resolving, and described HA fillers as generally safe and effective, with rare severe events lasting months and needing active treatment [8].

The most serious risk is accidental injection into or compression of a blood vessel, which can cause tissue death, vision problems including blindness and stroke; the FDA says these may be permanent [3]. Wikipedia notes that embolic complications are more frequent with autologous fat, followed by HA [2]. The FDA lists rare events as anaphylaxis, filler migration, leakage or rupture, hard nodules and death, and advises that removal can be hard for non-HA and permanent fillers [3]. Wikipedia describes hyaluronidase as the best option for dissolving HA filler when complications occur [30].

The FDA advises that fillers be injected by licensed providers, not self-administered, and not bought online because of counterfeit products, and has issued counterfeit-filler alerts in 2017 and 2018. It also states safety is not established in pregnancy or breastfeeding, in people under 22, with long-term repeated use or in people prone to keloids [3]. Wikipedia reports that a 2024 review raised concerns about long-term safety of the BDDE cross-linker [2]. Topical HA is generally described as well tolerated [4].

In the US the FDA regulates fillers as medical devices: approved absorbable fillers are for adults 22 and over, for facial wrinkles and folds and for augmentation of lips, cheeks, chin and the back of the hand, while the agency advises against use in the glabella, nose, forehead, neck and periorbital area and for body contouring, and states no fillers are approved for over-the-counter use [3]. In the EEA and UK, fillers are non-prescription medical devices needing a CE mark, which does not require proof of efficacy, with over 140 on the UK and European market against six in the US according to Wikipedia [2]. As a topical ingredient HA is a cosmetic ingredient [1].

HA is a humectant polymer that binds water. In cartilage, aggrecan binds to HA and the negatively charged aggregates draw in water, giving cartilage resistance to compression; in synovial fluid it contributes viscosity and lubrication [1]. In skin it supports hydration and keratinocyte migration during re-epithelialisation [1]. In wounds it supports cell migration and angiogenesis [1]. Low-molecular-weight fragments produced during inflammation can activate immune cells [31].

The repeating unit is a disaccharide of D-glucuronic acid and N-acetyl-D-glucosamine joined by alternating beta-1,4 and beta-1,3 bonds. Chains can reach about 25,000 repeats, with molecular weights in vivo from about 5,000 to 20 million daltons. Unlike other glycosaminoglycans it is made at the plasma membrane by hyaluronan synthases (HAS1, HAS2, HAS3) [1]. It can be modified at its carboxyl, hydroxyl and N-acetyl groups, including by cross-linking with BDDE or divinyl sulfone, to improve biocompatibility and durability [1][32].

Lip filler is the most visible cultural face of HA. Wikipedia notes that overfilled lips are often mocked online, sometimes called a trout pout, and that results depend heavily on provider skill [14]. HA fillers are part of the broader cosmetic procedure market discussed in appearance communities [7].

Forum material on strength-training sites treats HA mainly as a joint supplement or injection rather than a skin product. T Nation posters describe taking joint supplements containing HA, planning HA injections for knee or shoulder problems, and taking HA for connective tissue [9][10][11][12].

Cosmetic. A 2023 meta-analysis of 19 randomised trials on adverse events after facial HA filler injection [7]; a 2024 systematic review of 48 randomised studies [8]; a randomised prospective multicentre study of an HA micro-filler for superficial wrinkles [16]; a split-face trial of polynucleotide versus HA filler around the eyes in 27 participants [17]; and randomised trials of topical and oral HA described above [4][6][5].

Medical. Numerous randomised trials and reviews of intra-articular HA in knee, hip and temporomandibular joint osteoarthritis [19][20][21][22], and registered trials of viscosupplements and ophthalmic viscosurgical devices [23][24][25][26].
